meta.title: Use of Specimen Drying Rack in Pharmacognosy Laboratory

sections.purpose: To air-dry freshly collected plant specimens, herbarium sheets, and washed glassware in an organized manner to preserve morphological integrity and prevent mould growth prior to herbarium mounting or storage.
sections.scope: Applicable to Pharmacognosy laboratory for drying field-collected plant specimens, freshly pressed herbarium materials, and laboratory glassware after washing.
procedure: Inspect the specimen drying rack for cleanliness, structural integrity, and absence of rust or mould before use.
For fresh plant specimens: Remove excess moisture by gently blotting with absorbent paper (not rubbing — to preserve surface features).
For flat specimens (leaves, flowers): Arrange specimens on absorbent blotting paper and place between multiple layers of folded newspaper before hanging or spreading on the rack.
Position specimens on the rack with adequate spacing (at least 2–3 cm) between specimens to allow airflow on all sides.
Place the drying rack in a well-ventilated area — avoid high humidity environments.
Label each specimen position immediately with the collection number, plant name, collection site, and date.
Change the blotting paper every 24 hours for the first 3–4 days to speed up drying and prevent mould.
For succulent specimens (thick leaves, stems): Change blotting paper every 6–8 hours for the first 2 days.
Check specimens daily for signs of mould — remove affected specimens immediately and treat with 2% thymol in alcohol.
Drying is complete when specimens are stiff, crackle when bent, and have a constant weight.
For glassware: Place washed glassware inverted on the rack with adequate support — do not stack wet glassware.
Clean the rack after use with a damp cloth; dry thoroughly before storing.
Record all specimen accession numbers, drying dates, and final disposition in the herbarium logbook.
precautions: Place the drying rack away from direct sunlight — UV radiation and heat cause rapid colour loss and brittleness in herbarium specimens.
Maintain good air circulation — poor airflow causes mould growth within 24–48 hours in humid conditions.
Never use a hot oven for drying herbarium specimens — it destroys colour and makes specimens too brittle.
Label specimens before drying — wet labels cannot be written on and dry specimens may become confused.
Treat mould-affected specimens promptly — mould spreads rapidly in humid conditions.
Handle dried specimens with care — they are extremely brittle and break easily.
Fumigate the drying area periodically to prevent insect infestation of herbarium materials.
